item.title: No war? 377 US forces injured since July, 36 in last 2 weeks
item.description:
According to new data quietly added to the Pentagon's casualty base, there were 36 new injuries in the last two weeks, mostly Army, as fighting renewed between the United States and Iran in the Persian Gulf. This brings the total wounded count to 794 and 18 killed since the war began on Feb. 28.

The White House, including Vice President JD Vance just this week, likes to say this isn't "a war" but a "operation" but for the soldiers, sailors, and airmen who have been killed and injured, these semantics are meaningless. Just like the Pentagon's insistence that casualties that occurred before the July "ceasefire" must be classified under "Operation Epic Fury" and those after under "Overseas Operations." This is distinction without a difference.

Turns out the number of servicemen hurt in the latter — 377, with four dead — is almost as much as the former. In the pre-July period, there were 417 men and women injured and seven killed.

It is a grave insult to those who serve, and to the American people who support them, for politicians to downplay what is clearly a war in order to try and avoid the political cost and implications. Iran had been targeting U.S. facilities in Bahrain, Jordan, Iraq, and Kuwait in retaliatory strikes over the last week. The fact the Pentagon is not saying where, when, or how these men and women were wounded is a pathetic attempt to deter reality and ultimately it will backfire.

item.title: Ukraine war briefing: Zelenskyy links Russian strikes on Kyiv airports to US envoys’ visit
item.description:
Moscow attacked Kyiv and Boryspil international airports as talks yielded no evident change in Vladimir Putin’s peace demands. What we know on day 1,656

Russian attacks on Kyiv and Boryspil international airports were “clearly” a reaction to the possibility of the US negotiators flying to Kyiv after talks in Moscow, the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has said. On Saturday, Zelenskyy said Kyiv had “taken note of this Russian move, and next week we will adjust our operation accordingly regarding Russian airspace, which has become dangerous because of our drones and missiles in the sky. Of course, there are and will be no threats to diplomacy from our side.” Both airports service the Ukrainian capital.

There was no comment from the US envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, who were visiting Moscow for the first time since January. They flew out of Moscow soon after the talks and were ‌due to meet Zelenskyy in Kyiv ‌on Sunday. The Kremlin’s tone appeared unchanged. After three hours of talks, an aide to Vladimir Putin, Yuri Ushakov, said the Russian president had told the US pair that Russia was making “real progress” on the battlefield, was confident of achieving ⁠its goals, and stressed the necessity of addressing “all the root causes of the conflict”. Ushakov said ​the Americans had “outlined a number of ideas regarding possible avenues for a settlement”, but he did not say what those ideas were.

The air war between Russia and Ukraine has intensified as troops have struggled to make progress along the 1,250km (775-mile) frontline. Russia has recently been using fast-flying, jet-powered drones, and the recurring wail of air raid sirens has become part of daily life in Kyiv. Kremlin spokesperson ‌Dmitry Peskov posted online that Putin had ordered the military not to strike Kyiv for three days, starting at midnight on Saturday. However, he said Russia had not yet agreed to a broader three-day ceasefire. Zelenskyy has said Ukraine is prepared to refrain from strikes on Moscow through to Monday.

Russian attacks killed five employees and wounded five others at an industrial facility in the Dnipropetrovsk region, said the local military administration head, Oleksandr Hanzha. “A locksmith, an electrician, a plumber and a machinist. People of peaceful professions. They were simply working their shift. They were doing their job when enemy missiles cut off their lives.” Russia’s defence ministry said it had carried out strikes on two metallurgical plants that it claimed were sites for military production.

A 62-year-old man was wounded, and several homes and an apartment building damaged, in a separate attack on the region’s Nikopol district, Hanzha said. The city of Dnipro and the nearby Pidhorodne community were among the areas hit. One person died and five other were injured, including two men who were hospitalised in serious condition. A sixth civilian was injured in an attack on the Nikopol district.

Other deadly Russian attacks took place in Chuhuiv in Ukraine’s eastern Kharkiv region, on the Bucha district of Ukraine’s Kyiv region, and on a shopping centre in the southern Mykolaiv region. In Russia’s Belrogod region on the border with Ukraine, two people were killed and three others wounded by Ukrainian attacks on Saturday, local authorities said. Russia launched ballistic missiles from its Rostov and Voronezh regions and deployed 167 attack drones, Ukraine’s air force said on Saturday.

Inside Trump’s Massive Venezuela Oil Deal
item.description:
“A major oil agreement has been announced between the government of the United States and the [Venezuelan interim] regime of Delcy Rodriquez. I know what you [Venezuelans] are feeling, sadness, anger and that painful sense so familiar throughout our history that someone else is making decisions about what belongs to us in our name, without us. The true scope of this agreement is still unknown. Who is signing it? What exactly is being signed? Who is providing the funds? Who is offering the guarantees? How does this benefit Venezuelans? Quite rightly, this has sparked deep concern about its implications for our country's future.”

That was part of a statement to the Venezuelan people released last Thursday by María Corina Machado, a Venezuelan politician, activist, and prominent leader of the opposition to Venezuela’s interim-President Delcy Rodriguez. These were Machado’s first extended remarks about what President Trump has called “the biggest oil deal in world history.”

But as Machado so accurately observed, “We still do not know the true scope of this agreement,” nor, I will add, does anyone know if this deal will ever go into effect.

First, a bit of history, since I believe the Trump administration initial plan was described publicly back on January 9, when the President met with executives of 17 oil companies at the White House.

At that time, with Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro locked in a New York City jail, President Trump said, “American companies will have the opportunity to rebuild Venezuela's rotting energy infrastructure and eventually increase oil production to levels never ever seen before.”

“Our giant oil companies,” Trump said, “will be spending at least $100 billion of their money, not the government's money. They don't need government money, but they need government protection and need government security that when they spend all this money, it's going to be there.”

He added, “Venezuela [meaning interim-President Delcy Rodriguez] has also agreed that the United States will immediately begin refining and selling up to 50 million barrels of Venezuelan crude oil, which will continue indefinitely.”

Trump then made his pitch saying, “All of the companies here today are going to be treasured partners in bringing the nation of Venezuela back to life, restoring its economy and generating…tremendous wealth for the companies that are going in.”

At that session, Mark Nelson, vice chairman of Chevron, when called upon said, “For more than a century, Chevron has been a part of Venezuela's past. We are certainly committed to its present. And we very much look forward, as a proud American company, to help it build a better future.”

However, when Trump asked ExxonMobile Chairman and Chief Executive Officer Darren Woods to “say a few words,” the response was different.

Woods explained, “We have a very long history in Venezuela. In fact, we first got into Venezuela back in the 1940s. We've had our assets seized there twice. And so you can imagine to re-enter a third time would require some pretty significant changes from what we've historically seen here and what is currently the state.”

Apparently, over the past seven months more negotiations took place and on August 28, Trump announced on TruthSocial, “THE BIGGEST OIL DEAL IN WORLD HISTORY! At my direction, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, working closely with Highly Respected Interim President of Venezuela, Delcy Rodriguez, and, through a partnership with private business, have secured majority U.S. control of more than 65 BILLION BARRELS of proven Oil Reserves in Venezuela, at no cost to the American Taxpayer.”

Three days later, on August 31, the White House released a fact sheet with more details.

The fact sheet disclosed the Venezuelan interim government [Interim-President Delcy Rodriguez] has granted a privately-held oil company, North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP), 100-year concessions for 17 oil fields with proven reserves of approximately 65 billion barrels.

I should point out that Venezuela has some 303 billion barrels of proven oil reserves, the largest in the world, with Saudi Arabia second with 287 billion barrels. On the other hand, as of this year, the U.S, has only some 46 billion barrels of proven reserves, although this country is one of the world’s largest oil producers.

NABEP, based in Barbados, already was Venezuela’s second-largest private oil producer run by Leopoldo Alejandro Betancourt López. According to press reports, the 46-year-old Betancourt has a checkered background, but nonetheless was used by the Trump team in planning the U.S operation that seized former-President Nicolas Maduro, and afterwards served as a liaison figure with Delcy Rodriguez.

The White House fact sheet also said, “At no cost to the American taxpayer, NABEP has granted the Department of War’s Office of Strategic Capital (OSC) a 35% equity stake in its corporate parent, representing up to hundreds of billions in value and dividends for the United States.”

The OSC, started under the Biden administration, has up-to-now funded private companies developing certain needed military technologies. The Trump administration last year increased its legislative authority to support up to $200 billion in loans and loan guarantees, and recently has grown its staff to near 100 people.

But the OSC has never been prepared to deal with the role apparently to be required if, as the agreement apparently states, it would be a major stockholder in what could be one of the largest oil companies in the world.

Perhaps because of the proposed Venezuela deal, the OSC announced on August 17, it was going to establish “a panel of pre-qualified law firms (“Firms”) to act as its external transaction counsel.” The selected firms would then represent borrowers or others doing business with the OSC on a “Sponsor Pay Basis,” meaning that the legal fees and expenses of OSC for a transaction will be borne solely by the borrower or another third party and not by OSC, or any U.S. government entity.

An additional benefit from the deal to the U.S., according to the fact sheet is: “NABEP has also granted the U.S. State Department the right to purchase, at production cost, a guaranteed 20% of the off-take [contracted oil purchased] from all current and future fields NABEP will operate.” The State Department was also given “the right of first refusal to purchase the remaining 80% of its [NABEP’s] production,” according to the fact sheet.


It’s unclear why the State Department has this role other than Secretary Rubio was a negotiator of this deal and the State Department was named on Trump’s January 15, Executive Order to administer funds from current Venezuela oil sales being controlled at that time by the U.S.

As for NABEP -- the company itself -- the U.S. government was given “veto power over the appointment of any member of the board of directors,” plus “a majority of NABEP’s board of directors must be U.S. citizens,” the fact sheet said. Additional, according to the fact sheet, “the U.S. government’s agreement with NABEP is governed by U.S. law and is subject to the jurisdiction of U.S. courts.”

Naturally, questions about whether this agreement ever goes through have been raised.

On September 1, The Atlantic Council pointed out that the Pentagon’s OSC “has never been leveraged for a program like this or the management of such a vast equity stake in a foreign country’s national assets (assets which that country’s own constitution forbids the sale of).”

The Atlantic Council further said, “As in Venezuela, it is entirely plausible that future U.S. governments may likewise look askance at this agreement -- particularly if…it is not resulting in the massive oil production increases that are presently hoped for.”

For example, interim-President Rodriguez said during an August 29 television interview that the agreement could generate about $209 billion in ⁠revenue for Venezuela, based on a $65 per barrel oil price where some $19 per barrel would flow directly to Venezuela, to boost government revenue.

But others have questioned whether the Venezuelan government would actually get $19 per barrel if the U.S. exercised its right to buy 20 percent of production at cost.

Then there is the political opposition in Venezuela where leaders such as Machado have argued, “The wealth beneath our soil does not belong to an illegitimate regime. It belongs to the Venezuelan people.”

Machado added, “Venezuelans know there can be no development without strong institutions and a government elected by popular vote. That is the only real guarantee of success and stability for any large-scale investment.”

Last Wednesday, both Trump and Rodríguez brushed off questions about when the next Venezuelan election might be held.

Trump told reporters, “You had a very powerful, very nasty dictatorship in Venezuela – and they’re [the Venezuelan electorate] just not going to be ready for it yet, but soon.” With Energy Secretary Chris Wright, who was visiting Caracas, Rodríguez told reporters, “I have worked tirelessly to ensure that Venezuela is ready and prepared when the time comes for its electoral process.”

Elliott Abrams, who served as U.S. special envoy to Venezuela during Trump’s first term, has told the New York Times, “If an election is to take place in Venezuela, a nine-month runway for preparation is likely to be expected. Within the time period, Abrams said, “Here’s my fear: It makes us [the U.S.] Delcy’s partner, and gives the President a reason to want her to remain in power,” because she will do “whatever Trump tells her to do.”

Luis A. Pacheco, for 17 years an executive at Venezuela’s national oil company PDVSA and currently a nonresident fellow at Rice University’s Baker Institute for Public Policy, wrote last week in Americas Quarterly, “Little is known about how this deal will proceed, so important questions still need answers.”

Pacheco’s questions included, “Will NABEP sign this deal with PDVSA, the state oil company, making it more like a standard joint venture?...It’s still unclear whether NABEP can turn around and share ownership with the U.S. government, specifically with the Pentagon’s special unit originally designated as a counterpart to this pact. Beyond this critical aspect, there is also the question of NABEP’s financial and technical muscle. Will a firm that lacks these credentials be able to outsource to established oil companies to fulfill the contract’s scope?”

With experts raising such questions who can believe this “BIGGEST OIL DEAL IN WORLD HISTORY!” is going forward as currently planned?

For example, back during his January 9 press conference with oil company leaders at the White House, Trump announced that Venezuela had already given the U.S. 30 million barrels of what had been previously-sanctioned oil that it had on hand.

“That's about $4 billion worth,” Trump announced back in January, adding, “And it's on our way to the United States right now. And we want to thank Venezuela for that. And we're working very well with them, obviously, or they wouldn't have been so generous.”

There has been no accounting that I know of for that first gift of $4 billion worth of Venezuelan oil.

item.title: The India–China reset will continue at the BRICS summit
item.description:
The India–China reset will continue at the BRICS summit Expert comment jon.wallace 8 September 2026

So will disagreement over the purpose of BRICS.

India will host the 18th BRICS summit in New Delhi on 12–13 September at a time when the rest of the world is increasingly seeking to emulate its longstanding policy of strategic autonomy.

The Ukraine and Iran wars, continuing US–China rivalry, and the second administration of President Donald Trump have made New Delhi’s long-held commitment to strategic hedging and middle power diplomacy seem wise, if not urgent underpinnings for modern international relations.

However, even though the world may better reflect India’s worldview, New Delhi has found it difficult to apply its foreign policy approach to its BRICS chairmanship. 

Strain with Washington, reengagement with Moscow and Beijing

Recent Indian government actions confirm India’s continuing commitment to strategic hedging. New Delhi secured a string of resource deals during Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s recent visits to Australia, Indonesia and Uzbekistan. And it has agreed a number of trade deals, with nine in-progress or concluded since 2021 – including with the United Kingdom and European Union.

Trade negotiations with the United States continue, but relations with the second Trump administration have undoubtedly been strained, causing India to reinvest in other relationships.

Ony a few years ago, India was distancing itself from the China-led Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO): New Delhi hosted a low-key virtual summit in 2023. And Modi was absent from the summit in 2024. But more recently India has renewed its interest in the grouping and sought to improve relations with China and Russia. At this year’s SCO summit, Modi joined President Xi Jinping and President Vladimir Putin in signing the Bishkek Declaration, which condemned US-Israeli military attacks on Iran.

India’s BRICS agenda

India has consistently sought to be a ‘voice’ of the Global South, often by using its prominent position in platforms like the G20 (which it chaired in 2023) and the AI Impact Summit (which it hosted earlier this year).

Its BRICS chairmanship has continued these efforts. In August a joint declaration, the ‘Chennai Consensus’ made a commitment to collaborative research and innovation among developing countries on emerging technologies. The same month, BRICS trade ministers advocated preserving and revitalizing the multilateral trading system – a move likely aimed at the Trump administration’s disruptive tariff policies. And in June, BRICS agriculture ministers issued a food security declaration focused on the needs of developing countries.

The challenge for New Delhi is that it wishes to promote this worldview in a way that is non-Western but not explicitly anti-Western. To that end, it has sought to downplay some of the more controversial elements of the BRICS agenda. That includes a de-dollarization narrative championed by countries such as Brazil and Russia – an idea which last year caused President Trump to threaten to slap ten per cent tariffs on the BRICS in response.

Related work

How China–India relations will shape Asia and the global order

New Delhi emphasized that BRICS is not seeking to create a separate reserve currency to compete with the US dollar. It has instead reframed this as an effort to settle bilateral trade in national currencies and use digital payments to reduce transaction costs for cross-border trade.

India has also promoted a more benign worldview, reflected in the BRICS slogan of ‘Humanity First’ and the theme of ‘Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability’. But this seems increasingly outdated given recent geopolitical developments, in particular US military action against Venezuela and Iran.

India’s position can appear out of sync in a forum whose membership includes countries with more overtly anti-Western agendas, including China, Russia and Iran. And two other BRICS countries, South Africa and Brazil, have suffered high profile diplomatic disputes with the US.

A key watchpoint at this summit will therefore be how New Delhi reconciles its efforts to stay on good terms with Washington with calls by BRICS member states to voice opposition to US actions. As Chair and host of BRICS, India’s actions will be more scrutinized, and it will be reluctant to oversee the production of a statement similar to Bishkek. 

Multilateral symbolism

These tensions are exacerbated by the broader challenges of maintaining cohesion among the 11 BRICS member states. Tensions between Iran and the UAE, for instance, are high as a result of the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. Relations between Addis Ababa and Cairo have been strained by Ethiopia’s Nile dam project. Saudi and UAE interests conflict on relations with Israel and other issues. And India has its own longstanding frictions with China to manage, although there have been signs of improvement over the last two years.

Additionally, among the founding member states – Brazil, Russia, India, and China – there is still no consensus on what the BRICS stands for. Brazil and India see it primarily as an economic-driven initiative. China and Russia see it through more of a geopolitical lens. Beijing in particular is increasingly using forums like the BRICS to promote its own worldviews through its Global Development, Security, Civilization and Governance Initiatives. Meanwhile, Moscow has used the BRICS to seek alignment with the Global South as it is ostracized by the West following its invasion of Ukraine.

From New Delhi’s perspective, BRICS has been moving in the wrong direction. BRICS was established as a reaction to calls for a greater voice for the Global South in multilateral institutions, with a focus on development and governance. India would like to build on the organization’s earlier achievements, including the establishment of the BRICS New Development Bank and Contingent Reserve Arrangement in 2015.

The difficulties BRICS has speaking with one voice could affect its future. In the two decades since the BRICS was formed, newer groupings have emerged, such as the recent defence pact between Pakistan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia. There is a possibility that such regional, exclusive groupings may become more important actors than expansive and inclusive groupings like BRICS.

Such factors mean that BRICS expansion is likely to take a backseat for the foreseeable future. Instead, the focus will probably be on socializing new members into the organization.

Efforts to expand the BRICS mandate will likely be limited to engagement with other forums in the Global South. However, even this is challenging. Bangladeshi Prime Minister Tarique Rehman – whose country holds the chair of BIMSTEC, a South and Southeast Asian regional forum – has not yet accepted an invitation amid tensions with India.

Bilateral substance

The real action at the BRICS Summit will take place on its sidelines with a series of bilateral meetings. In particular, the meeting between Modi and Xi is likely to further advance the ongoing reset in bilateral relations and build confidence. A meeting in August between the Chinese foreign minister and Indian national security advisor made notable progress on their longstanding border dispute. And Xi’s upcoming visit to India – his first since 2019 – will reportedly include a 400-person delegation.

In this context, the recent accomplishments of BRICS have come from its convening power. It was a Modi–Xi meeting at the 2024 BRICS Summit in Russia that set the ball rolling on resetting the relationship.

Ultimately, the Global South remains an amorphous concept. There remains little clarity on what advocating its interests actually means, beyond making vague calls for a more equitable distribution of power in a multipolar global order. The BRICS summits needs to move behind platitudes and statements towards more substantive outcomes if it is to be seen as a real contender in global governance.

At the summit, New Delhi will seek to return BRICS to its original development-focused agenda, as reflected in its Economic Partnership Strategy 2030. However, this threatens to be hijacked by fissures among its members and calls for another statement condemning US attacks on Iran. But the group needs more than opposition to the US to define a better vision for the Global South. This entails moving beyond what it stands against to what it stands for.

item.title: Pakistan’s New Military Order Is a Warning for Washington
item.description:
In Washington, Field Marshal Asim Munir increasingly looks like the man who can make Pakistan useful to the United States. Pakistan has just written Munir even more deeply into the architecture of the state as he now sits atop a legally centralized command that reaches conventional forces, strategic systems, and the prime minister’s national-security advice. Munir, now formally serving as Chief of Defense Forces, speaks directly with President Donald Trump and has become Washington’s principal channel for engaging Tehran.

The latest restructuring of Pakistan’s military command has actually made the opposite case. The 27th Constitutional Amendment, followed by legislation passed this month to implement the new command architecture, has concentrated unprecedented authority in Munir’s hands. Yet his military cannot stabilize Pakistan-administered Kashmir, cannot contain the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) and Baloch insurgents, and has still signed a mutual-defense pact with Turkey and Saudi Arabia—dubbed the Mecca Accord—that could drag it into distant crises. For the world, treating Pakistan as a reliable intermediary in negotiations with Iran would be a mistake of timing and of judgment as the state becomes more militarized domestically, more ambitious diplomatically, and increasingly overstretched militarily.

A Field Marshal Above the State

In November 2025, the 27th Constitutional Amendment abolished the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Committee and created the office of Chief of Defense Forces (CDF), held concurrently by the army chief. The restructuring was completed with another step this month when Pakistan’s parliament passed the Defense Forces Act 2026 and amendments to the National Command Authority Act, providing the statutory framework for Munir's new position and headquarters. The new architecture gives the CDF a central role in operational command and joint military coordination across the armed forces.

The new law places the army, navy, and air force under a unified Defense Forces Headquarters commanded by Munir. He is designated the prime minister’s principal military adviser on national security and defense and exercises operational command and control across the services with sweeping personnel authority—hiring, firing, retirement, and extensions. Amendments to the National Command Authority law align nuclear and strategic command with the same hierarchy, with a new four-star Commander of the National Strategic Command sitting alongside the CDF. The significance goes beyond military administration, as Munir now occupies a position from which military command, strategic security policy and foreign-policy influence converge. He is not constitutionally Pakistan's president or prime minister, but describing him merely as a military officer increasingly misses the political reality. Such radical consolidation of power in Pakistan’s civil-military landscape matters for Washington because the United States is increasingly treating Munir personally as a diplomatic asset. Therefore, Washington must factor in that any “Pakistani” channel on Iran now runs, in practice, through a single command that answers first to its own institutional interests.

Consolidation Without Control

The strongest argument against treating Munir's Pakistan as a reliable strategic partner can actually be found inside Pakistan itself. The military has acquired unprecedented institutional power, yet the state remains under enormous security pressure. Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies data show that July 2026 was the deadliest month of the year, with 606 people killed in militant violence and counter-militancy operations, including 112 security personnel and 401 militants. The violence is concentrated precisely in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KPK) and Balochistan, where Pakistan's military has struggled for years. Such a security landscape is a sustained counterinsurgency burden for a military that is simultaneously presenting itself as a regional security provider.

The latest round of violence in Pakistan-Administered Kashmir has added another layer of security burden for an overly stretched military. In the surrounding areas of Rawalkot, Pakistan-administered Kashmir, protests led by the Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC) escalated after authorities outlawed the movement under anti-terrorism laws, suspended mobile data and internet services, and deployed security forces ahead of a JAAC-organized June 9 strike. According to a local human rights watchdog report dated August 8, at least 89 civilians died in Pakistan-administered Kashmir as a direct result of the state’s brutal crackdown on unarmed protesters.

Locals demanded cheaper power from dams that generate electricity for Pakistan, representation that is not diluted by non-resident seats, and an end to elite privileges. The state’s answer was lethal force, sedition cases, travel advisories, and the criminalization of a civic coalition that had previously extracted limited subsidies through protest. That is the Balochistan playbook applied to a territory Pakistan still markets internationally as “Azad” or free. It did not produce consent but a banned movement, underground leaders, and a legitimacy crisis inside a territory the army treats as strategic hinterland. If Munir’s new command structure was meant to deliver coherence, Kashmir shows the opposite, where a security establishment that can rewrite the constitution faster than it can address bread-and-butter revolt. An army that cannot manage a rights protest in Muzaffarabad and Rawalakot without mass casualties is not an army that can be trusted to midwife a delicate regional settlement with Iran or be a reliable partner for the so-called Mecca Accord.

Pakistan’s Utility Should Not Be Mistaken for Reliability

US talks with Iran already sit on a knife-edge of “Economic D-Day” politics, Hormuz control, and factional vetoes inside Tehran. None of this means the United States should abandon Pakistan as that would be strategically simplistic. Pakistan remains nuclear-armed, sits between Iran, Afghanistan, India and China, and retains diplomatic access across the Muslim world. Its ability to communicate with Tehran can be useful, particularly when direct US-Iranian channels are blocked. Three factors that Washington should use to distinguish between utility and reliability while dealing with Munir’s Pakistan:

First, Munir’s legal supremacy does not equal policy reliability. A CDF who is also army chief, principal adviser, and strategic-command fulcrum will filter any Iran file through the army’s need to look indispensable at home—that incentive points toward swagger, not quiet brokerage.

Second, Washington cannot treat Islamabad’s internal security failure as a side issue. An institution that answers civic protest in Kashmir with live fire and a terrorist ban is the same institution that would be asked to counsel restraint, verification, and de-escalation with Iran. The record says it prefers coercion when legitimacy frays.

Third, Munir’s capacity is already committed to a plethora of insurgencies. TTP and Baloch campaigns consume attention, ammunition, and men. A Mecca clause adds hypothetical external obligations without adding spare combat power. A partner that is simultaneously over-centralized and overstretched cannot deliver the one thing Washington would need from it: consistent, low-drama influence on a file that can restart a wider war.

If the United States wants Pakistan to help mediate with Iran, it should judge Islamabad by the outcomes of that diplomacy, not by the personal access Munir enjoys in Washington. And if Washington wants Pakistan as a security partner, it should look beyond the impressive authority of its field marshal to the increasingly unstable state that authority is supposed to govern. A stronger Pakistani army does not automatically produce a stronger Pakistan. And a stronger Munir does not automatically produce a more reliable American partner.

item.title: Will the UN vote to sustain Haiti’s Gang Suppression Force?
item.description:
Will the UN vote to sustain Haiti’s Gang Suppression Force? Expert comment jon.wallace 10 September 2026

Sustaining the force is essential. But so too are funding commitments to restore the health and education services Haitians desperately need.

On 30 September the UN Security Council will vote on renewing the Gang Suppression Force (GSF) for Haiti. 

Now is not the time to pull the plug on GSF and its security effort. If anything, the Security Council vote should be an opportunity to swiftly renew the force and then confront an additional uncomfortable issue: How can development assistance be mobilized for Haiti, among a fractured international donor community?

‘Haitian-led’

After the 2021 assassination of President Jovenel Moïse, a mantra took hold among diplomats that any solution to the country’s spiral of chaos and crime needed to be ‘Haitian-led’. It’s a nice phrase, intended to reassure sceptics that a solution would not be imposed on Haiti. 

But how are Haitians supposed to lead?

Haiti hasn’t had an election since 2016. There is no elected government at any level – local, departmental, parliamentary or presidential. Political parties are in disarray. Many are still controlled by the same distrusted leaders that have dominated Haitian politics for decades. 

Indeed, according to a Chatham House-QQ survey, more than 75 per cent of Haitians don’t trust their political leadership. And civil society remains fragmented, weak and often distant from political power – despite years of international development support. 

That leaves the international community with continued responsibility to help get Haiti back on its feet. And that means doing much more than funding the vital GSF.

Respondents to the Chatham House-QQ survey identified education and healthcare as priorities in re-establishing security: 69.1 per cent and 67.3 per cent respectively. Development assistance will be needed to deliver these basic services. But where will it come from? 

Fragile progress

Chatham House’s survey was conducted in May 2026. That was a month after the first GSF contingent of 400 Chadian troops arrived in Haiti and following operations by the Haitian National Police (HNP) against the gangs that control almost all of Port-au-Prince. An estimated 1,300 gang leaders and members were killed in those operations.  Those efforts were assisted by divisions within the coalition of gangs that had come to dominate parts of Haiti and its economy.  

At the time of the survey, a slight majority of Haitians (50.7 per cent) were starting to believe that their communities had become safer. But support for the GSF was mixed: 49.5 per cent of voting age respondents said they approved or strongly approved of the multinational force. 

Related work

What Haitians want from the next phase of UN and international support

Unsurprisingly, that support was greater among Haitians living on the front lines of the insecurity, in or close to gang-controlled areas, where more than 67 per cent approved or strongly approved. 58.4 per cent of Haitians between the ages of 18 and 29 – a key demographic for Haiti’s recovery and future – also showed strong support for the GSF. 

Yet 54.2 per cent of Haitians polled don’t believe the GSF can accomplish its mission. 

At best, Haitians are modestly optimistic. But the window of opportunity to channel even this limited support may close quickly. The Security Council must act to build on what fragile progress has been made. 

The development need 

The importance of effectively addressing Haiti’s failed state and humanitarian disaster goes beyond Haiti and the security risks it presents to the Caribbean. Much is at stake for the United Nations, and the future of international cooperation.

The GSF resolution of 2025 was a rare victory for the UN after past resolutions had been vetoed by China and Russia. And it sets a model for how the international community, including many countries from the Global South, can still collaborate to respond to humanitarian tragedies.  

Kenya and Chad contributed troops. Canada committed funding and was instrumental in pushing the GSF approval over the line last year. Germany, Qatar and the US have also contributed funding. Mexico, Colombia, El Salvador, Jamaica and Brazil have made in-kind contributions through training, materiel and advisors. 

The Haiti resolution demonstrates that the international community can come together, even in this semi-ad hoc fashion, to respond to humanitarian crises – even when faith in the international system is waning. The courageous work of UN officials and diplomats posted in Haiti coordinating this effort is a testament to the enduring belief in global institutions and the principles under which they were founded. 

But the work is only beginning. If the GSF can establish itself, the next phase will bring new challenges, mainly related to development. Without the US Agency for International Development (USAID), who will step up to coordinate the next essential stage of Haiti’s recovery? The US now lacks the resources, commitment and moral authority to convene a donors’ conference and mobilize resources and commitments for Haitians’ needs. Are solutions still possible without the might of the US to drive them?

Who will step up? 

When the Security Council gathers to approve the renewal of the GSF, the hope is that their discussion will progress beyond security to the broader challenges of how to restore a shattered and brutalized country. Reaching agreement on a security force is a beginning only. New commitments must be made to invest in Haiti’s education, healthcare, and economic future.

The US’s commitment to focus on security and ‘gang suppression’ first was necessary. And its pushing through of a Security Council resolution that would focus on protecting Haitians was both successful and laudable. 

But there is now a need to work in parallel on social and economic development and the rebuilding of Haiti’s battered physical and institutional infrastructure. That will take funding by a broad group of donors and agreement on where and how to invest to the best effect.  

It will also require more than the kind of concessional loans normally offered by development banks. Haiti’s interim government is too broken to commit to such debts. Instead, those banks should work with supportive governments to develop an incentive-based, conditional partnership with the interim government – or its successor. That would involve agreeing to release funds when Haiti’s government reaches benchmarks in security, fiscal, healthcare, education and macroeconomic reform.

The US Development Finance Corporation (DFC) must also play a key role. The well-bank-rolled DFC can provide investor insurance and concessionary loans to encourage private investors to fill the gaps left by the elimination of USAID. Frankly, they will probably do it better than USAID because of their focus on investment, trade and results. 

However, that will require a more concentrated effort by the DFC to focus on Haiti. The DFC’s mandate to ‘mobilize private capital to advance US foreign policy’ can equally apply to other donors, including government development agencies, private foundations and multilateral development banks. 

Rebuilding Haiti and protecting the security of Haitians by battling gangs is not just a US foreign policy interest. Haiti has already become a vector for gun smuggling, narcotics trafficking and other illicit activities. Further state collapse would only bring greater insecurity, and not only to its neighbours in the Caribbean (including UK Commonwealth countries), Mexico and the US. The longer the crisis goes on the greater the risk that Haiti becomes a stateless hub for transnational crime – affecting every country with an Atlantic coast.

item.title: U.S. makes progress in reopening the Strait of Hormuz, but the Iran war is far from over
item.description:
In recent weeks, the United States has succeeded in loosening Iran’s grip over the Strait of Hormuz while virtually shutting down Iran’s own oil exports, accelerating its economic free fall.

But the war launched by the U.S. and Israel in February — intended to last a few weeks — is still far from over, and the stalemate is costly for both sides. An agreement reached in June quickly crumbled, with no sign of diplomatic progress since then. Low-level fighting persists, and the U.S. does not seem to have an exit strategy.

The mounting economic pressure on Iran has yet to stoke an uprising, and if its leaders are backed into a corner, they may opt for military escalation rather than capitulation. Their Houthi allies in Yemen have meanwhile stepped up attacks on Saudi Arabia, helping to push oil prices back up.

The price of a barrel of Brent crude, the international benchmark, surged above $100 this week, and diesel — heavily used in transport and farming — hit a record, potentially stoking inflation. U.S. President Donald Trump has acknowledged that gas prices are likely to stay high through the midterm congressional elections.

“Unfortunately, the U.S. is not winning in the war with Iran despite its limited success in loosening Iran’s grip over the strait and the devastating impact on Iran’s economy,” said Mona Yacoubian, a Middle East expert at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington.

“Iran shows no sign of backing down, and instead has demonstrated a willingness to not only fight back, but escalate wherever it can. The war is likely to be protracted with no clear victor.”

Iran loses leverage as oil moves through the Strait of Hormuz

Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz — through which a fifth of the world’s traded oil and gas transits in peacetime — in the opening days of the war, using the worldwide economic shock as leverage. Meanwhile, it continued to export its own oil, mainly to China.

But in recent weeks, the balance has reversed. A U.S. blockade has virtually halted Iran’s exports, while the American military has facilitated greater exports by Gulf countries, according to figures compiled by Homayoun Falakshahi, an oil expert at Kpler, a global trade monitor.

He found that Iran’s oil exports had dropped from 1.85 million barrels a day last spring to around 255,000 in August. Exports of non-Iranian oil rose from 300,000 barrels a day at the height of the war to 8.4 million in September, and exports through alternative routes took that number to 10.8 million.

U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright boasted of similar figures on Sunday, saying “we’re probably two-thirds or more of preconflict flows.” Non-Iranian exports were at around 14 million barrels a day before the war, according to Falakshahi.

But the increased flow depends on a major U.S. deployment in the strait that has strained the military’s resources. The unpopular war has already cost U.S. taxpayers more than $37.5 billion and left 18 U.S. service members dead, and is expected to weigh on Republicans in November’s election.

Tehran could escalate in other ways

The tightened blockade and new U.S. sanctions are already taking a heavy toll on Iran’s economy, driving up prices and causing even longer lines outside gas stations.

But so far, it’s shown no sign of pushing the country’s increasingly hard-line leaders to make concessions on the Strait of Hormuz, Iran’s disputed nuclear program or its support for armed groups in the region.

“Washington’s main problem is that it still lacks a theory of victory: More ships are getting through, and Iran is hurting, yet none of that has produced a political outcome,” said Ali Vaez, an Iran expert at the International Crisis Group think tank.

Iran has continued to attack ships in the strait, drawing limited U.S. strikes on its coastal areas and then responding with missile attacks on Arab countries hosting U.S. forces. Trump recently dismissed the conflict as “small potatoes.”

But with the U.S. supply of sophisticated interceptors showing strain, Iran could be tempted to escalate its attacks — or respond through regional proxies.

The Iran-backed Houthis launched a wave of attacks on Saudi oil facilities this week as part of a conflict that goes back more than a decade but has heated up in recent weeks. The Houthis are also attacking Saudi shipping, threatening its oil exports and a crucial trade route through the Bab el-Mandeb chokepoint leading to the Red Sea and the Suez Canal.

The Houthis have damaged Saudi Arabia’s Jizan refinery, a large supplier of diesel and jet fuel to Europe, Falakshahi said. The volume of Saudi oil passing through the Bab el-Mandeb bound for Asia has plunged from around 3.4 million barrels a day in June to just 128,000 in August, according to Kpler’s figures, though it has recovered slightly to some 700,000 barrels per day in September.

“Tehran has repeatedly signaled that it will respond to growing U.S. pressure by moving up the escalation ladder, not by backing down,” Danny Citrinowicz, a senior researcher at Israel’s Institute for National Security Studies and a former Israeli intelligence officer focused on Iran, wrote on X.

“Iran will not simply accept an indefinite maritime blockade, nor will it allow Washington to impose mounting economic costs without imposing costs of its own,” he wrote.

Krauss reported from the Middle East for more than 20 years, with postings in Cairo, Jerusalem and Baghdad.

—Joseph Krauss, Associated Press

item.title: Ukraine war briefing: Poland calls for ‘double’ support to Kyiv after Russian train attack
item.description:
Polish minister denounces ‘escalation’ after strike near border with UK’s Boris Johnson and ex-CIA chief David Petraeus nearby. What we know on day 1,664

Poland and Ukraine have denounced Russian strikes close to the Polish border as an “escalation” in the war after a train was targeted while former British prime minister Boris Johnson and ex-CIA director David Petraeus were at a border station nearby. The escalation should lead to allies to “double” their support for Ukraine, Poland’s foreign minister said in Kyiv. “This was just a few hundred metres from the Polish border, this affects the safety of my countrymen,” Radoslaw Sikorski said. Polish prime minister Donald Tusk chaired an emergency meeting in Warsaw after the strikes, warning he expected Russia to escalate the war “in the coming weeks”. He added: “We cannot exclude that the escalation will also affect our territory … I hope not.”

Poland and Ukraine said the Kyiv-Warsaw passenger train was struck just 2km from the Polish border, reporting no casualties. Shortly beforehand a diplomatic train was at Yagodyn station including Johnson and former Swedish prime minister Carl Bildt as well as security advisers from several EU member states, while former CIA director David Petraeus was aboard another train at the station when the attack occurred, the Ukrzaliznytsia rail operator said. It did not say how far the officials were from the train struck.

Zelenskyy said Moscow had “deliberately” struck the locomotive. “It is precisely to prevent these strikes from spreading further into Europe that Ukrainian men and women fight every day, give their lives, and do not allow the aggression to expand,” the Ukrainian president said. Ukrainian Railways said Johnson and Petraeus may have been the target, report Amy Hawkins and Charlotte Higgins. Ukrainian foreign minister Andrii Sybiha said the attack was “Putin’s terror knocking directly on the doors of the EU and Nato”.

Donald Trump has called on Zelenskyy to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries and other infrastructure used to produce and distribute diesel, saying the attacks were causing a global shortage. “Mr Zelenskyy has to do one thing – he has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia,” Trump told reporters in Ireland after diesel prices in the US hit a record high on Friday. “We spoke to Mr Zelenskyy about it. There are plenty of other targets. Don’t hit diesel fuel, because that’s hurting the world.” Kyiv says Russia’s oil industry funds and fuels Moscow’s war on Ukraine.

Trump sought to tie Ukraine’s attacks on Russian refineries to rising oil prices, saying it was these attacks and not America’s ongoing conflict with Iran that were responsible for price rises. “This isn’t done by the Middle East, this is done by what’s happening with Russia and Ukraine,” the US president said. According to a report published on Friday by the International Energy Agency, net exports of diesel and oil from the Gulf countries in August stood at “just over a quarter” of what they were before the war on Iran began in February. “Disruptions to Russia’s refining system and a near-halt to product exports following intensified Ukrainian attacks have compounded these losses,” the agency wrote.

The Kremlin said negotiations with Ukraine and the US on the war could take place in October. “We do not rule out such a possibility – we are talking about the foreseeable future,” Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said, cited by Russia’s Ria and Tass news agencies. Zelenskyy said separately he would be willing to meet Putin at the G20 summit in Miami in December, but Peskov said that was “impossible”, repeating Moscow’s demand that a meeting could only take place in the Russian capital. Putin has repeatedly rejected offers for face-to-face talks with the Ukrainian president.

Zelenskyy has imposed sanctions on a former press secretary, ⁠accusing her and nine others of spreading Russian propaganda and of supporting Russia’s aggressive policy ⁠towards Ukraine. Yuliia Mendel, who ⁠worked with ​Zelenskyy from 2019 to 2021, before Russia’s invasion – responded with a message on Facebook saying it ⁠was unconstitutional to impose sanctions on Ukrainian citizens. She did not comment on the specific accusations.

item.title: The Houthis’ capture of Mocha has transformed the war in Yemen – and the geopolitics of the Red Sea
item.description:
The Houthis’ capture of Mocha has transformed the war in Yemen – and the geopolitics of the Red Sea Expert comment thilton.drupal 14 September 2026

Iran and its allies can now exert pressure on two strategic maritime chokepoints, with global implications. A more coherent international approach to Yemen is needed.

The Houthi armed group recently captured the strategic port city of Mocha in southwestern Yemen and advanced along the coast of the Bab al-Mandab Strait. This represents the most consequential change in territorial control in Yemen for years.

For Yemen, the offensive risks reopening a war that never formally ended but had become significantly less violent since the UN-mediated truce of 2022. For the wider region, the implications are also massive.

The Houthis’ new territorial position gives them much greater ability to influence maritime shipping through Bab al-Mandab, the narrow passage connecting the Gulf of Aden to the Red Sea and ultimately the Suez Canal. 

Together with Iran’s disruption of the Strait of Hormuz, Iran and its allies now have the capacity to exert pressure on two of the world’s most strategically important maritime chokepoints.

The Houthis have also launched attacks into Saudi Arabia, including against energy infrastructure, that have reportedly injured civilians. This also constitutes an escalation in the conflict and poses questions for Riyadh and its US ally. 

The fragmentation of Yemen’s anti-Houthi camp

Houthi forces, who control most of western Yemen, made a rapid push down the Red Sea coast last week. Government-aligned forces withdrew as the Houthis seized Mocha, surrounding areas and nearby islands. 

The Houthis benefited from surprise and military preparation. But the offensive also exposed the fragmentation of the anti-Houthi camp.

Government-aligned forces face coordination problems. The anti-Houthi forces include a variety of autonomous armed groups who were previously supported by different regional patrons and had competing political ambitions. Saudi attempts to bring them under a more coherent command structure since early 2026 have not erased years of fragmentation.

Meanwhile, the Houthis used the period of relative calm following the 2022 truce to recruit and mobilize personnel, improve domestic weapons production and expand their missile and drone capabilities. As a result, the Houthis now have more advanced capabilities than government forces in several areas. 

Bab al-Mandab, the Red Sea and the Horn of Africa 

The immediate international question is what the Houthis intend to do with their strengthened position around Bab al-Mandab.

The Houthis previously claimed they do not intend to impose formal transit fees on vessels passing through Bab al-Mandab. These assurances should be treated cautiously. There are indications that, since beginning their attacks on Red Sea shipping in 2023, the Houthis have been extracting informal payments from some shipping agencies in return for safe passage. 

The Houthis have also said that they are only attacking Saudi-linked ships in the Red Sea. However, a ship carrying Saudi oil may be owned, operated, financed, insured or chartered by companies in several different countries. It might also be delivering goods, or oil, to various countries. 

Houthi attacks on Saudi shipping therefore affect commercial interests far beyond Saudi Arabia, including in Europe and China.

Related work

The Houthi Red Sea blockade: Will collective maritime security be defended, or break down?

The Houthi advance also changes the security calculations of states with strategic interests in the Horn of Africa. 

Djibouti is just around 20 kilometres from Perim Island, which the Houthis now reportedly control. That places an armed movement with increasingly sophisticated drone, missile and maritime capabilities extremely close to a country that hosts US, Chinese, French, Italian and Japanese military bases. Other countries including Turkey and the United Arab Emirates also have significant security and commercial interests in the region. 

For now, the Houthis’ calculation is likely to be one of controlled escalation: converting military momentum into political and economic leverage without provoking an international response large enough to reverse their gains. But Yemen can no longer be treated as a distant theatre.

Trump faces difficult choice

Saudi Arabia has vowed to respond to Houthi attacks on its territory. Riyadh recently signed a mutual defence treaty with Turkey and Pakistan, but does not appear to have publicly called on either for assistance. 

The US, a close Saudi ally, reached a truce with the Houthis in May 2025, after conducting air strikes against the group following its attacks on shipping in the Red Sea. 

For US president Donald Trump, the recent Houthi advance creates a difficult dilemma. Trump has a close relationship with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, and the US retains a fundamental interest in Saudi security. At the same time, Washington has strong incentives to avoid reopening a direct war with the Houthis.

The existing truce gives both sides reasons for restraint. For Trump, preserving that arrangement helps keep the US away from another costly Middle Eastern military confrontation while it remains engaged in the Strait of Hormuz.

The Houthis have equally strong incentives to not be drawn into conflict with the US. The 2025 US air campaign against the Houthis caused serious damage. They have little interest in inviting a repeat.

This creates a peculiar situation: Washington and the Houthis both have reasons to avoid attacking one another, even while the Houthis increase pressure on one of the US’s closest regional partners.

That equilibrium, however, may not hold. If the Houthis escalate attacks on Saudi territory, especially if they attempt even limited ground incursions across the border, Washington could find itself pulled towards confrontation.

Yemenis pay the greatest cost 

Lost beneath the geopolitical consequences is the most predictable outcome of renewed war: Yemenis themselves will suffer most.

The country enters this phase of conflict with divided institutions, an economy devastated by more than a decade of war and declining international humanitarian support.

In Taiz alone, almost 50,000 people have reportedly been displaced since 3 September. In Mocha, the humanitarian consequences are particularly alarming. With health facilities collapsing or becoming inaccessible, local media reports indicate that more than 240 pregnant women in the region face the looming prospect of giving birth without access to functioning medical care.

Further disruption to ports, roads and supply chains will also drive up food, transport and fuel prices in a country heavily dependent on imports. 

While this new international dimension of Yemen’s war makes the country strategically more important to the world, it should not overshadow the plight of ordinary Yemenis. 

The need for a coherent international approach

Governments have tended to treat Saudi-Houthi negotiations, maritime security, humanitarian access to Yemen, Iran negotiations, the Yemeni government and wider Red Sea maritime security as separate issues. That approach is becoming increasingly difficult to sustain.

The Houthis are now able to influence global shipping, energy markets, Gulf security, the Horn of Africa and the calculations of major powers. A more coherent international approach is therefore needed.

For Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) states in particular, the latest escalation should be a warning. The GCC has not formulated a coherent policy on Yemen, influenced by disagreements between Gulf states and their different relationships with Yemeni factions. But the Houthis’ recent advances impact the entire GCC, so a Gulf-wide approach is needed. 

Recent developments should also challenge the idea that the Houthis can be contained through a collection of transactional arrangements. Bilateral maritime security deals may protect one country’s ships, while negotiations may temporarily calm one frontline. Military strikes can degrade individual capabilities.

But these approaches operate in silos. The Houthis do not. The movement simultaneously functions as a governing authority, an armed non-state actor, an Iranian regional ally and an increasingly important influence on maritime security.

The main policy challenge is therefore whether regional and international actors are prepared to develop a coherent approach to Yemen that connects the country’s political settlement with wider security issues in the Gulf, the Red Sea and the Horn of Africa. Ultimately, ignoring a crisis in Yemen does not contain it. It is only a matter of time before it becomes an international crisis.
